posts.caption: Loading the trailer at 6:15 on a frost morning is a negotiation I have lost more times than I'd like to say. Our smallest pony treats the ramp like a rumor. He'll sniff it, circle it, and look at me as though I've asked him to board a boat. I tried the lead rope, the whistle, and a bucket of grain held at arm's length. Eventually my neighbor walked over with the feed bin in both hands and set it just inside the door. He walked up the ramp like he'd planned the whole thing.
posts.first: My first trailer was a borrowed two-horse with a rusted fender and a floor I checked twice every time. I loaded a mare in it once in a downpour while wearing my husband's raincoat. She walked on like it was her idea. I've been chasing that day ever since.

posts.caption: Show mornings start in the dark. The alarm goes off at 4:00, the coffee goes into a thermos, and somebody has to be in the barn with a braiding kit and a headlamp. Our chestnut mare held perfectly still for forty minutes, like a woman getting a wedding updo. Then I turned my back to grab the hay net and she reached for it with the grace of a champion. By the time we pulled into the showground, one braid had come loose and she'd decided it was an improvement. The judge never said a word.
posts.first: I braided my first mane at fourteen with a borrowed comb and a roll of yarn. It took ninety minutes and looked like a bad haircut. Nobody said anything, and the horse still won her class. I've thought about that kindness every show morning since.

posts.quote: The water trough froze solid overnight. I chipped it open with a hammer and the horse looked at me like I'd done it on purpose.
posts.first: Eleven winters in, I keep a small hammer by the water trough, a kettle on the stove, and an old towel in the truck. The horse keeps his opinion. Some mornings I think the ice is only there to remind me he's in charge, and I'm just the staff.

posts.caption: Every lesson barn has one horse that has taught the whole county to ride. Ours is a dappled gray gelding who retired three years ago and kept his job. Last month a young woman pulled into the lot in a muddy truck with a trailer behind it. She walked straight to his paddock before she even checked her own mare. He ambled over to the fence and stood like a monument while she scratched his cheek. They didn't say anything. The new mare could wait. This was the one who'd taught her where to put her hands.
posts.first: My first instructor passed away years ago, but I still tuck my hair under my helmet the way she showed me. It takes ten seconds and no mirror. Some things stay in the hands. I think horses know it before we do.

posts.caption: The barn whiteboard has a turnout schedule, color coded, laminated and initialed. Our plump bay mare has never once read it. I opened her stall at 9:00 and found her flat out in the straw with the barn cat on her hip, both of them looking offended at the interruption. The grain was still warm. I stood in the doorway for a full minute deciding whether to argue. Then I brought a second cup of coffee into the aisle and moved her turnout to 11. It's now been 11 for three weeks.
posts.first: I wrote the first turnout schedule myself on a paper plate with a marker. The horses ignored it for a whole winter. Eventually I stopped fighting the paper plate and started following the horses. The barn has run smoother ever since, and I've never admitted it to anyone.

posts.caption: The farrier's truck pulled in at 6:40, which is early even by his standards, and I could already hear Red thinking about it. He's shod her for seven years and he knows the drill: set the tools down slowly, say hello, and never mention her feet before breakfast. She stood like a statue for all four hooves. Then she turned her head, looked at his pocket, and waited. He apologized and went back to his truck for the peppermints. I paid the invoice, and Red inspected her new shoes like a woman reading a contract.
posts.first: The first farrier I ever hired told me a horse's feet are the foundation of everything else. I nodded politely and didn't understand him for ten years. Now I leave a thermos on the tailgate and the peppermints in my coat. It's the cheapest advice I ever took.
